`Catalog/Applications/MordellInfiniteOrbit.lean`), which established, all sorry-free:

* the square-denominator law `den x = e²`, `den y = e³` for every rational point of
  `y² = x³ + N` (`N ∈ ℤ`);
* exact invariance of the `ℓ`-part of `den x` under doubling for odd `ℓ`, and `×4` growth at
  `ℓ = 2`;
* the complete local law `ℓ ∣ den x(2P) ↔ ℓ ∣ den x(P) ∨ ℓ ∣ num y(P)` at good primes `ℓ ≥ 5`;
* **closure of the denominator kernel under the chord** (`kernel_stable_add`), hence
  `ℓ ∣ den x(kP)` for all `k ∈ ℤ` once it holds for `k = 1`, at *every* prime;
* the **apparition index law** (`den_apparition_index`): the set of `k ∈ ℤ` at which a prime
  appears in the denominator is exactly `mℤ` for some `m ∈ ℕ`, with `m(7) = 2` and `m(13) = 3`
  on `E_55, P = (9,28)`;
* the exact `2`-adic growth `v₂(den x(2^k Q)) = v₂(den x(Q)) + 2k`, and its consequences:
  `P = (9,28)` has infinite order and `E_55(ℚ)` is infinite;
* infinitely many *distinct* multiples of `P` whose denominator carries the good prime `7`.

Two conjectures of the previous cycle (old C1 closure, old C5 exact `2`-adic jump) are therefore
now theorems. The list below is the refreshed one; each conjecture is falsifiable by a single
explicit rational point or by one finite computation.

## C1. Ultrametric valuation law for the chord

**Statement.** Let `N ∈ ℤ`, let `ℓ` be an odd prime and let `P₁, P₂` be rational points of
`E_N` lying in the denominator kernel at `ℓ`, with `v_ℓ(den x(P₁)) ≠ v_ℓ(den x(P₂))`. If
`P₁ + P₂` is affine with `x`-coordinate `x₃`, then
`v_ℓ(den x₃) = min(v_ℓ(den x(P₁)), v_ℓ(den x(P₂)))`; and if the two valuations agree, then
`v_ℓ(den x₃) ≥ v_ℓ(den x(P₁))`, with equality unless `ℓ ∣` an explicit resultant.

**The key insight is** that `kernel_stable_add` already produces the chord `x`-coordinate as an
explicit ratio `A/B` of integers in the coprime parametrisation `x = a/e²`, `y = b/e³`, so the
`min` law is a statement about the `ℓ`-adic sizes of the three summands of `A` — no formal-group
machinery is needed, only a term-by-term valuation count.

**Why now?** The closure statement is proved, so the qualitative half of the ultrametric picture
is settled; what remains is exactly the quantitative refinement, and the integer identity that
carries it is already in the file as `chord_den_not_dvd_of_kernel`.

## C2. Every good prime appears in the orbit of one non-torsion point

**Statement.** Fix `N = 55` and `P = (9,28)`. For every prime `ℓ ∉ {2,3,5,11}` there is `k ≥ 1`
with `ℓ ∣ den x(kP)`, and the apparition index `m(ℓ)` of `den_apparition_index` equals the order
of the reduction `P̄` in the finite group `E_55(𝔽_ℓ)`; in particular `m(ℓ) ∣ #E_55(𝔽_ℓ)` and
`m(ℓ) ≤ ℓ + 1 + 2√ℓ`.

**The key insight is** that `ℓ ∣ den x(kP)` says exactly that `kP` reduces to the point at
infinity mod `ℓ`, so the index produced abstractly by the subgroup argument must coincide with
the order of the reduced point — turning an existence statement into a computable quantity
bounded by Hasse.

**Why now?** The index `m(ℓ)` now exists as a theorem rather than a heuristic, and two of its
values are pinned down (`m(7) = 2`, `m(13) = 3`); identifying it with the order of `P̄` is the
single missing bridge between the elementary denominator theory here and reduction mod `ℓ`.

## C3. The denominators form an elliptic divisibility sequence

**Statement.** For an integral point `P` of `E_N` there are integers `d_k > 0` with
`den x(kP) = d_k²`, `den y(kP) = d_k³`, and `(d_k)` satisfies
`d_{m+n} d_{m−n} d₁² = d_{m+1} d_{m−1} d_n² − d_{n+1} d_{n−1} d_m²`. In particular
`d_m ∣ d_n` whenever `m ∣ n`.

**The key insight is** that `mordell_den_pow_structure` already produces the single integer
sequence `d_k` unconditionally, and the divisibility `d_m ∣ d_n` for `m ∣ n` is precisely the
apparition-index law refined from "which primes" to "with which multiplicity".

**Why now?** The apparition index law gives the prime-by-prime shadow of `d_m ∣ d_n`; Mathlib
carries division polynomials for Weierstrass curves, so the full recurrence can be attacked
directly instead of through `ℓ`-adic estimates.

## C4. Quadratic growth of the denominators, and density one

**Statement.** With `P = (9,28)` on `E_55`, `log den x(kP) ∼ 2 ĥ(P) k²`, and consequently the
set `S(P) = {ℓ prime : ∃ k, ℓ ∣ den x(kP)}` has natural density one among the primes.

**The key insight is** that the exact `2`-adic law already proves *linear* growth of one
valuation along one sub-orbit (`v₂ = v + 2k`), which is the degenerate case of the canonical
height asymptotic; upgrading `k ↦ 2^k` to all `k` is what converts linear growth in `log` into
the quadratic law.

**Why now?** `mordell_55_point_infinite_order` removes the only hypothesis such a statement
needs (non-torsion), and it is proved here without heights — so the height asymptotic is now a
statement about an object already known to be infinite rather than a conditional one.

## C5. Denominator data cannot recover the factorisation of `N`

**Statement.** For semiprime `N = pq`, the multiset of primes dividing `den x(kP)` for
`k ≤ K` is, for every fixed `K`, computable from `N` alone in time polynomial in `log N` *given
oracle access to the points* — and contains no subsequence that isolates `p` or `q` more often
than the trivial guess. Concretely: there is no function of `{den x(kP) : k ≤ K}` that outputs a
nontrivial factor of `N` for a positive proportion of semiprimes.

**The key insight is** that the apparition index law makes the appearance of *every* prime — good
or bad — governed by the same mechanism (the order of the reduced point), so the primes dividing
`N` enjoy no structural distinction inside the denominators; the survey data (`p` present 54.5%,
`q` present 0%) is exactly what this predicts.

**Why now?** With closure, the index law and the infinite-orbit theorem in place, the barrier can
be stated as a theorem about the index function `ℓ ↦ m(ℓ)` rather than as a collection of
counterexamples; the missing step is a uniform bound showing `m(p)` and `m(q)` are not
distinguishable from `m(ℓ)` for good `ℓ`.
